A new collection edited by Edward Fullbrook and Jamie Morgan, [23 Responses to Economics’ Biggest-ever Question](https://rwer.wordpress.com/2026/07/14/23-responses-to-economics-biggest-ever-question/), puts the most consequential unresolved question in economic thought on the table: whether an economy organized around growth can continue within the biophysical limits of a finite planet — and what it means for the discipline if it cannot. Subtitled "Economics and the Biophysical Limits to Economic Growth," the volume's framing rests on a claim made by natural science: the global economy caused the climate crisis, and the crisis, now in an accelerating phase, threatens the economy's own existence. For a discipline that has "loosely guided the global economy's national economies" for over a century, that is not a refinement. It is a structural challenge.

## A Century of Guidance, a Question Left Unasked

Twenty-three separate responses to a single framing question, assembled in one volume, signals that Fullbrook and Morgan understand this not as a debate with a settled answer but as a live rupture in the discipline's foundations. That it is framed as the biggest-ever question economics has faced, and that it generates this density of differentiated response, reflects a shift in urgency — one driven by the crisis entering its accelerating phase.

The collection's central claim, grounded in natural science rather than economic theory, is that the relationship between growth and its biophysical consequences has reversed direction: growth caused the crisis; the crisis now constrains growth. What has changed is the insistence that economics, as the discipline that has guided the global economy for over a century, must now account for what natural science has established — rather than defer it to another field.

## The Policy Architecture Already Built on a Bet

The difficulty is that major institutional decisions have not waited for this reckoning. Green growth — the premise that economic expansion can be decoupled from resource use and made consistent with ecological stability — is not a fringe hypothesis. [Green growth](https://unevenearth.org/2022/10/green-growth/) by Winne van Woerden for Uneven Earth documents it as the governing assumption embedded in the European Green Deal, the Paris Agreement, IPCC reports, and the US Inflation Reduction Act, promoted by leading multilateral organizations and treated as common sense across national and international policymaking.

The institutional bet embedded in those frameworks is that the answer to the collection's central question is yes — growth can continue, cleanly enough, within biophysical limits. If the 23 responses suggest otherwise, the implications don't settle in academic journals. They land in every policy instrument that has already staked its architecture on decoupling working at the required scale.

## Growth Mania Beyond the Material Economy

The logic the collection scrutinizes is not confined to resource extraction. [Growth mania is fueling dangerous advances in AI – and its existential risks](https://www.resilience.org/stories/2026-07-09/growth-mania-is-fueling-dangerous-advances-in-ai-and-its-existential-risks/), published in Resilience, frames AI development as "the apex of growth mania" — decisions made by a small number of tech elites without the consent or interests of the broader population in mind. The pattern is structurally similar to the one the collection examines: growth imperatives generating consequences externalized onto those who didn't drive the growth, with no internal mechanism registering accumulating cost until the feedback becomes impossible to absorb.

Whether the same discipline that missed this dynamic in the material economy is equipped to track it in digital infrastructure is not a question the current volume takes on. But the logic of compounding externalities the collection foregrounds runs through both domains.

## What 23 Responses Open

The collection resolves nothing, and it doesn't claim to. What the format makes visible is that the question is now being engaged at scale within mainstream economics — that biophysical limits have generated enough serious response to constitute a volume of 23 differentiated voices, not a pamphlet from the ecological economics margin.

That shift might matter less for what economics does next than for what it becomes harder to ignore. Every growth projection, every policy framework, every national economic plan runs on assumptions — stated or not — about what physical systems can sustain. The collection marks the moment when those assumptions became the question, not the premise.

SUMMARY:

The manuscript's core content — the Fullbrook-Morgan collection, its natural-science framing, and the green growth policy context — is accurately rendered and well-attributed. The piece fails in its third substantive section, where the writer extends the AI source into an analytical framework the source summary does not provide and misattributes the quoted phrase to the wrong subject. That defect is contained to one section, which makes this a REVISE rather than a REFUSE. The final section also carries confident assertions about the collection's historical significance that outrun the available evidence. The rest of the piece is sound.

---

FINDINGS:

The lede and first two sections hold up. The collection's title, subtitle, editors, and framing claim — that the global economy caused the climate crisis and the crisis now threatens the economy's existence — are all drawn faithfully from the `rwer.wordpress.com` source, including the near-quote about economics having "loosely guided the global economy's national economies for over a century." The green growth section accurately credits Winne van Woerden writing for Uneven Earth, and the claims about the European Green Deal, Paris Agreement, IPCC reports, and Inflation Reduction Act are supported by the source summary, which names those instruments explicitly.

The failure begins in the section "Growth Mania Beyond the Material Economy."
